title: What Qatar GP date firmness means for F1 rescheduling canceled Bahrain or Saudi Arabia races
content:
The president of the Qatar motorsport federation has said his country’s upcoming grand prix will not shift its date if Formula 1 attempts to reschedule a canceled 2026 Middle East race.

This makes a move to create another triple-header between the planned events in Baku and Singapore across late September and early October more likely.

The scheduled F1 events in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April were canceled in the aftermath of conflict between the United States and Israel and Iran breaking out on February 28.

Derek Chang, the CEO of F1 commercial rights holder Liberty Media, then said in May “it might be possible to reschedule one race toward the end of the season.”

As previously reported by The Athletic, this would be a complicated process, as adding a race at the very end of season would create an unprecedented four races in successive weekends and cause issues for the events long scheduled in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, which round out the 2026 campaign.

The stance of the Qatar Motor and Motorcycle Federation (QMFF) reflects the position of Formula One Management, which has formed what CEO Stefano Domenicali called “plans” in May in the event “the world, not only for the racing, will go back to (a) normal situation.”

The main focus of these plans would be to create a new triple-header of races in Azerbaijan, then either Bahrain or Saudi Arabia on October 4, then move on to Singapore — around the planned events in Baku and Singapore on September 26 and 11 October respectively.

In an interview with The Athletic at the 2026 Le Mans 24 Hours last weekend, QMMF president Abdulrahman bin Abdullatif Al Mannai replied “no” when asked if the Qatar GP race date of November 29 would shift to accommodate a rescheduled race.

He added: “I don’t see it will shift, because we are really (only) before Abu Dhabi, which is the last round. I think it’s really difficult to shift any dates right now.”

When contacted by The Athletic, a spokesperson for the F1 organization, which is in charge of assigning the F1 calendar each year, highlighted Domenicali’s previous comments.

Al Mannai, who was at Le Mans to oversee the Team Qatar GT3 entry, formed in conjunction with the Italian Iron Lynx team, also said that Qatar is not facing a cut-off on whether the race could go ahead in any case, given the continued uncertainty in the region.

The U.S. and Iran have agreed a memorandum of understanding for terms to end the conflict, which includes a 60-day window for talks over the latter’s nuclear ambitions. It is also yet to be signed, although this is planned to take place on Friday.

“We don’t have any cut-off, because we are actually ready to host these events,” said Al Mannai. “Our circuit is ready, we have everything lined up. At any moment, we’re happy to organize these races. So, so far, we don’t have a cut-off date or anything like that.

“But we will see. We’ll go through in the summer and we will see.”

Also speaking at Le Mans last weekend was FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem. He told media including The Athletic that “we still have to make a decision in a month or two” on the final make-up of the 2026 calendar, around the possibility of a race being added back in.

“Because logistically you don’t want to go on and then it’s canceled at the end of the day,” he added. “Because you have travel, (the) logistics of sending everyone there suddenly. To us, in the FIA, the protection of humans and the safeguarding, it’s one of our priorities.”

Assuming that the situation in the Middle East stabilizes, Qatar is now scheduled to hold three major motorsport events in five weeks late in 2026.

The canceled World Endurance Championship and MotoGP rounds are currently slated to be held instead at the Lusail track on Oct. 24 and Nov. 8 — five and three weeks before F1 arrives respectively.

“We are ready to go,” Al Mannai said of this run. “But like everybody else, we’re waiting for the situation to get better.”
